subject: ela
description: Students determine the central idea of an informational text and analyze how that central idea is conveyed and developed through particular details such as facts, examples, statistics, expert statements, and the way information is organized. They distinguish a central idea (the main point the author develops about the topic) from the topic itself (a one-word or one-phrase subject) and from a single supporting detail. They also write or select an objective summary that captures the central idea and the key supporting points in a logical order while leaving out personal opinions, judgments, and reactions. Every item embeds the full article, passage, or excerpt it depends on, so the student needs nothing external to answer it.
subSkills: Distinguish the central idea (the main point the author develops) from the topic (a one-word or short-phrase subject such as recycling or the moon)
Determine the central idea of an informational text using evidence from across the whole passage, not just one paragraph
Identify the specific details (facts, examples, statistics, expert quotations, comparisons) that convey or develop the central idea
Explain how a chosen detail supports or develops the central idea
Distinguish an objective summary from a personal opinion, judgment, or reaction
Write or select an accurate, objective summary that states the central idea and key supporting points in a logical order and excludes personal commentary

problemArchetypes.name: Determine the central idea
problemArchetypes.example: Read the short article, then answer: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage? Answer choices offer one true central idea (the main point the details build toward) plus distractors that are topics, single details, or unsupported claims.

problemArchetypes.name: Central idea versus topic
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage. One answer names a topic (such as 'honeybees') and another states a central idea (such as 'Honeybees play a vital role in growing the food people eat'). The student selects the option that is a central idea rather than a topic.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the detail that develops the central idea
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage. The student is told the central idea and must choose which specific detail (a particular fact, statistic, example, or quotation) best develops or supports that central idea.

problemArchetypes.name: Explain how the central idea is conveyed
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage, then explain how the author conveys the central idea through a particular detail, naming the detail and connecting it to the main point about the topic.

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the objective summary
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage. Several candidate summaries are given; one states the central idea with key supporting points and stays objective, others insert opinions ('this proves we must act now'), omit the central idea, or add information not in the text. The student selects the objective summary.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the opinion in a summary
problemArchetypes.example: Read a passage and a draft summary. The student identifies which sentence or phrase in the summary is a personal opinion or judgment rather than an objective statement of what the text says.

Easy.description: A short, single-topic informational passage (roughly 60 to 120 words) with an explicit, clearly signaled central idea embedded in the item, often stated near the beginning or end. The task is to identify the stated central idea, distinguish a central idea from a topic, or pick the obvious objective summary. One concept is tested and the supporting detail is direct.
constraints: Stimulus is a 60 to 120 word informational passage included in the prompt
Central idea is clear and reinforced by a topic sentence or a direct restatement
Identify-level task: select the central idea, the topic-versus-central-idea choice, or the matching objective summary
Distractors are surface-level (a topic word, a single restated fact) and easy to rule out
Minimal inference; the main point is nearly stated in the text

Medium.description: A multi-paragraph informational excerpt (roughly 150 to 250 words) with a central idea that must be inferred by combining several supporting details rather than reading one topic sentence. The task requires analysis: connecting a particular detail to the central idea, or building or selecting an objective summary that orders the key points and strips out opinion.
constraints: Stimulus is a 150 to 250 word informational excerpt included in the prompt
Central idea is implied across several facts, examples, or paragraphs, not stated in a single sentence
Analyze-level task: match a central-idea-developing detail, or choose the summary that is both complete and objective
Distractors include a plausible-but-too-narrow central idea, a summary missing a key point, and a summary containing one opinion
Moderate inference across more than one part of the text

Hard.description: A longer or more complex informational passage (roughly 280 to 400 words) that may include multiple subtopics, technical vocabulary, contrasting information, or a shift from problem to solution. The task requires evaluation: judging which statement most fully captures the central idea, explaining how a specific detail develops it, or distinguishing a strong objective summary from one that subtly inserts judgment, overweights one detail, or misorders the key points.
constraints: Stimulus is a 280 to 400 word informational passage included in the prompt, possibly with technical terms or contrasting information
Central idea is subtle or develops across subtopics; a too-narrow detail could be mistaken for the main point
Evaluate-level task: select the best full statement of the central idea and justify with a detail, or pick the truly objective and complete summary

Distractors are sophisticated: a partially true central idea that captures only one section, a summary that buries an opinion in objective wording, a summary that reorders or overweights one supporting point
Requires inference across the whole passage and attention to how the author builds the main point

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses the topic with the central idea, naming a one-word or short-phrase subject instead of the main point the author develops
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects 'recycling' or 'the rainforest' as the central idea instead of a complete statement such as 'Recycling at home can meaningfully reduce the amount of waste sent to landfills'

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student mistakes a single supporting detail for the central idea, choosing one fact or example rather than the broader point it helps prove
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects 'A single oak tree can drop ten thousand acorns in a year' as the central idea instead of the larger point the detail supports, such as 'Oak trees survive by producing far more seeds than can ever grow'

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student picks a central idea that is too narrow, covering only one paragraph or section instead of the whole passage
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a claim that fits only the opening section instead of the central idea developed across the entire text

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student chooses a detail that is vivid or surprising but does not actually develop the central idea
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects an interesting side fact or a colorful example as the central-idea-developing detail instead of the fact or statistic that directly supports the author's main point

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student includes personal opinions or judgments in a summary, treating reactions as part of what the text says
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a summary containing 'everyone should start composting today' or 'this is the most important issue of our time' instead of an objective account of the central idea and key points

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student writes a summary that omits the central idea or adds information not in the text, so it is inaccurate even if opinion-free
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a summary that lists scattered facts without stating the main point, or one that invents a detail the passage never provides, instead of the accurate, complete summary

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats the first or last sentence as automatically the central idea or summary, mistaking one line for the main point of the whole text
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects the opening sentence or a single quoted line as the central idea or summary instead of a statement that captures the main point and key supporting details of the full passage
